### Introduction

Here we are working on our second project for ST 558, back to the old grindstone... We will work on building a shiny app to allow a user to explore a data set of our choosing.

For this project, I decided to use player-level data from the 2025-2026 UEFA Champions League (UCL) season (highest level of professional soccer) to build my app (Source: FotMob). The criteria for a player being included in the data set is that they had to make at least 1 appearance (as either a starter or a substitute) in the UCL season at any point.

Let's start by downloading the data into our session:

```{r Libs}

library(utils)
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(ggrepel)

```

### Download Data

We are pulling in 2 separate data sets below:

1) Player Matches: This data set contains match-level information from our 2025-26 UCL season for each player that registered at least 1 appearance. This includes information like player rating, minutes played, goals scored, expected goals, etc. 

2) Player Season: This data set contains season-level information from our UCL season for each player that registered at least 1 appearance. This includes information like total number of goals, total minutes played, expected goals per 90 minutes, etc. 


```{r Pull data}

player_matches <- read.csv("data/player_matches.csv")
player_season <- read.csv("data/player_season.csv")

```

### Static Exploration

Let's start light with some 1-way contingency tables to explore our data. Personally, I am a fan of Borussia Dortmund, who are a German Club in the Bundesliga, which is the highest division in German professional soccer. I am interested in the number of appearances, number of goals, and number of assists held by every player on the team:


#### 1-Way Contingency Tables

```{r Dortmund 1-way CT}

#Number of Appearances
dortmund_apps <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  group_by(player_name) |>
  summarize(Appearances = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(Appearances)) 

gt(dortmund_apps) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Appearances - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
    )

#Total number of goals scored
dortmund_goals <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  group_by(player_name) |>
  summarize(Goals = sum(goals__value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Goals)) |>
  mutate(Goals = coalesce(Goals, 0))

gt(dortmund_goals) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Goals Scored - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
  )
  

#Total number of assists
dortmund_assists <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  group_by(player_name) |>
  summarize(Assists = sum(assists__value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Assists)) |>
  mutate(Assists = coalesce(Assists, 0))

gt(dortmund_assists) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Assists - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
  )

```

Note that Goals and Assists are NA for our friend Gregor Kobel due to his position as Goalkeeper. Certainly not impossible for him to have a goal or an assist, but that was the default value in the data for goals and assists for goalkeepers if they did not have any goals or assists, and I think it makes sense for our purposes to leave it that way for the time being given how rare these occur. 

#### 2-Way Contingency Tables

Now let's take a look at the same metrics, but add another layer of detail and see whether or not the players were starters or substitutes:

```{r Dortmund 2-way CT}

#Number of Appearances
dortmund_apps_by_sub <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  mutate(starter = if_else(starter == "True", "Starter", "Substitute")) |>
  group_by(player_name, starter) |>
  summarize(Appearances = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Appearances)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = starter, values_from = Appearances) |>
  mutate(Starter = coalesce(Starter, 0), Substitute = coalesce(Substitute, 0))

gt(dortmund_apps_by_sub) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Appearances by Appearance Type - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
  ) 


#Total number of goals scored
dortmund_goals_by_sub <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  mutate(starter = if_else(starter == "True", "Starter", "Substitute")) |>
  group_by(player_name, starter) |>
  summarize(Total_Goals = sum(goals__value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Total_Goals)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = starter, values_from = Total_Goals) |>
  mutate(Starter = coalesce(Starter, 0), Substitute = coalesce(Substitute, 0))

gt(dortmund_goals_by_sub) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Goals by Appearance Type - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
  ) 


#Total number of assists
dortmund_assists_by_sub <- player_matches |>
  filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
  mutate(starter = if_else(starter == "True", "Starter", "Substitute")) |>
  group_by(player_name, starter) |>
  summarize(Total_Assists = sum(assists__value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Total_Assists)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = starter, values_from = Total_Assists) |>
  mutate(Starter = coalesce(Starter, 0), Substitute = coalesce(Substitute, 0))

gt(dortmund_assists_by_sub)  |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Number of Assists by Appearance Type - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player"
  ) 

```

To be honest, these goal and assist numbers don't look too hot for a Top-Flight German team that is (supposedly) meant to be a top 2 team in Germany, and a top 12 club in Europe. Luckily, our data (and many other sources of soccer data), track player match ratings for each game, which scale from 1-10. In the FotMob rating system, each player starts their appearance with a 6.0 rating, which increases or decreases based on their actions during the game. Let's take a look at the average match rating across the season for the Dortmund players, and compare them to the other teams:

#### Numerical Summaries

```{r Dortmund Numerical Summaries}

#Let's start with the average match rating for each player at Dortmund across the season, then the team as a whole:

dortmund_avg_match_rating <- player_matches |>
     filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
     drop_na(rating_title__value) |>
     group_by(player_name) |>
     summarize(num_games = n(),
               avg_match_rating = round(mean(rating_title__value), 2), .groups = "drop"
               ) |>
     arrange(desc(avg_match_rating))


gt(dortmund_avg_match_rating) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Match Rating - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player",
    avg_match_rating = "Average Match Rating",
    num_games = "Number of Games Played"
  )

#Let's also look at these average match ratings as starters and as subs:
dortmund_avg_match_rating_by_sub <- player_matches |>
     filter(team_name == "Borussia Dortmund") |>
     drop_na(rating_title__value) |>
     mutate(
       starter = if_else(starter == "True", "Starter", "Substitute"),
       num_games = n(),
       .by = player_name
     ) |>
     group_by(player_name, starter) |>
     summarize(
       num_games = first(num_games),
       avg_match_rating = round(mean(rating_title__value), 2),
       .groups = "drop"
     ) |>
     arrange(desc(avg_match_rating)) |>
     pivot_wider(
       id_cols = c(player_name, num_games),
       names_from = starter,
       values_from = avg_match_rating
     )

gt(dortmund_avg_match_rating_by_sub) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Match Rating - Borussia Dortmund",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    player_name = "Player",
    num_games = "Number of Games Played"
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Starter, Substitute),
    missing_text = "—"
  )
 

```

Unfortunately, the data does not contain player ages, but one thing I notice at a glance is that a lot of the players with the higher ratings are on the younger side. This is likely biased though, since these younger players are given less opportunities to play and therefore have a lower sample size of games, but it is still encouraging to see that they are playing well when given their opportunities. Let's see how the teams average rating compares to other teams in the league:

```{r League Numerical Summaries - Average Rating}

league_average_rating <- player_matches |>
  drop_na(rating_title__value) |>
  group_by(team_name) |>
  summarize(
    num_ratings = n(),
    avg_match_rating = round(mean(rating_title__value), 2),
    median_match_rating = round(median(rating_title__value), 2),
    sd_match_rating = round(sd(rating_title__value), 2),
    min_match_rating = min(rating_title__value),
    max_match_rating = max(rating_title__value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_match_rating))


gt(league_average_rating) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Match Rating Summaries - All Teams",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    team_name = "Team",
    avg_match_rating = "Average Match Rating",
    num_ratings = "# of Match Ratings",
    median_match_rating = "Median Match Rating",
    sd_match_rating = "Match Rating Standard Deviation",
    min_match_rating = "Lowest Match Rating by 1 Player",
    max_match_rating = "Highest Match Rating by 1 Player",
  )

```

Above we can see the total number of match ratings (or the total number of player appearances across the entire season) for each team, and their average team match ratings across the entire season. The top 3 teams, Bayern, PSG, and Arsenal, all made last years UCL semi-final, as one might expect based on their ratings. Interestingly though, Athletico Madrid was the 4th team to make the semis with the 11th ranked average match ratings for their players. An underdog that appeared to over perform compared to other teams. Internazionale, Newcastle, and Tottenham all had relatively underwhelming performances relative to their average match ratings, as they were all knocked out in the Round of 16 or prior. 

It could also be interesting to check out which teams ran the most distance on average, and which teams created the most chances on average. We are using averages here since many teams do not play the same number of games:

```{r League Numerical Summaries - Distance and Chances Created}

league_avg_distance <- player_matches |>
     drop_na(physical_metrics_distance_covered__value) |>
     group_by(team_name) |>
     summarize(num_games = n(),
               avg_distance_covered = round(mean(physical_metrics_distance_covered__value), 2), .groups = "drop"
               ) |>
     arrange(desc(avg_distance_covered))


gt(league_avg_distance) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Distance Covered - All Teams",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    team_name = "Team",
    avg_distance_covered = "Average Distance Covered Per Player Per Game (km)",
    num_games = "# of Match Ratings"
  )


league_avg_chances <- player_matches |>
     drop_na(chances_created__value) |>
     group_by(team_name) |>
     summarize(num_games = n(),
               avg_chances = round(mean(chances_created__value), 2), .groups = "drop"
               ) |>
     arrange(desc(avg_chances))
 
gt(league_avg_chances) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Chances Created - All Teams",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    team_name = "Team",
    avg_chances = "Average Chances Created Per Player Per Game",
    num_games = "# of Match Ratings"
  )

```

The distance covered table tells us something interesting: the amount of distance that a team covers during a game does not necessary correlate with team success. The UCL champions, PSG, did have quite a high average distance covered per player per game, but there are other teams that went far in the tournament that were much lower on the list, like Barcelona (dead last in average distance covered!) and Arsenal (middle of the pack). The 3 highest distance-covering teams did not make it past the round of 16, with only 1 even making it there. 

The table for chances created is a different story. Chances created translate to goals scored, which translates to games won. This is, in my own personal opinion, the best proxy for whether or not a team will be successful. PSG, the eventual winners, had the highest average number of chances created per player per game, with Bayern in 3rd and Arsenal just behind both in 8th. Athletico Madrid again here showing that they over performed, having the 16th highest number of chances created per player per game. 

Looking at Dortmund in both cases, they placed 10th in Distance Covered and 19th in Chances Created...lots of running but very little chance creation. Not the best formula for success, and certainly not the best formula for keeping players motivated to win. The last thing any player wants is to be running the entire game with little to no opportunities to put chances away. Hopefully things improve this season, but for now, the running will continue until chance creation improves...

### Plots

Let's take a look at the above tables and summaries visually:

#### Bar Charts

```{r Dortmund Data Vis Bar Charts}

ggplot(dortmund_apps,
```

```{r Dortmund Data Vis Boxplot and Dumbell Plot}
dortmund_dumbbell <- dortmund_avg_match_rating_by_sub |>
```

#### Scatterplot

```{r League Data Vis Scatterplot}

league_summary <- league_average_rating |>
  select(team_name, avg_match_rating) |>
  left_join(
    league_avg_distance |>
      select(team_name, avg_distance_covered),
    by = "team_name"
  ) |>

    league_avg_chances |>
      select(team_name, avg_chances),
    by = "team_name"

  ggplot(aes(
    x = avg_distance_covered,

  theme_minimal() +

    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    aes(label = team_name),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = 20
  )

```

#### Heatmap

```{r League Data Vis Heatmap, fig.width=10, fig.height=12}

league_heatmap_data <- league_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      avg_match_rating,
      avg_distance_covered,
      avg_chances
    ),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  group_by(Metric) |>
  mutate(
    Standardized_Value = if (
      all(is.na(Value)) ||
      is.na(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) ||
      sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE) == 0
    ) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      as.numeric(scale(Value))
    }
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    Metric = recode(
      Metric,
      avg_match_rating = "Average Match Rating",
      avg_distance_covered = "Average Distance Covered",
      avg_chances = "Average Chances Created"
    )
  )

team_order <- league_summary |>
  arrange(avg_match_rating) |>
  pull(team_name)

league_heatmap_plot <- league_heatmap_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = Metric,
    y = factor(team_name, levels = team_order),
    fill = Standardized_Value
)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#555555",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#FDE100",
    midpoint = 0,
    na.value = "gray90"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Team Performance Across Key Metrics",
    subtitle = "2025-26 UEFA Champions League",
    x = "Performance Metric",
    y = "Team",
    fill = "Standardized\nValue"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

league_heatmap_plot



```
